edges.effect_quant: The 2024 meta-analysis of 24 trials and 4,919 adults found no early advantage at 2-4 or 6 months, but social-support-based interventions showed significant benefits by the end of intervention and at 3-month and 6-month follow-up, suggesting that peer-connected support matters most once maintenance pressure begins.
edges.population: adults with overweight or obesity trying to maintain prior weight loss
edges.mechanism: Peer support helps weight-loss maintenance by replacing solitary self-control with shared accountability, normalization, and repeated social reinforcement. That matters more in maintenance than in acute weight loss, because the main challenge is not learning what to do but continuing to do it when external structure fades.
edges.summary: The strongest evidence suggests peer support does not produce a dramatic early maintenance effect, but it does improve the odds of holding on to weight loss over time. Large maintenance trials and newer meta-analysis both point toward the same pattern: regular human contact and group accountability do not prevent all regain, yet they do reduce how much weight tends to come back.
edges.caveats: This literature blends partner-based, couple-based, and group-based support models, so not every peer format is equally effective. Some trials also compare peer contact against already active maintenance programs, which makes the added value of support look smaller than it would against a true minimal-control condition.
